items.sentence_raw: Artificial intelligence (AI) can already predict the future.
Police forces are using it to map when and where crime is likely to occur.
Doctors can use it to predict when a patient is most likely to have a heart attack or stroke.
Researchers are even trying to give AI imagination so it can plan for unexpected consequences.
Many decisions in our lives require a good forecast, and AI is almost always better at forecasting than we are.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says AI is *'almost always better at forecasting than we are'* — **'forecasting'** means predicting the future. This matches heading **iii** — *'The superiority of AI projections over those made by humans'* — where **'projections'** means predictions. So the answer is **iii**.

items.sentence_raw: Yet for all these technological advances, we still seem to deeply lack confidence in AI predictions.
items.explain: Q33: The passage starts by listing AI's amazing abilities, then says *'Yet for all these technological advances, we still seem to deeply lack confidence in AI predictions'* — **'lack confidence'** means there is a problem with trust. This shows the writer is **highlighting the existence of a problem**, not solving it or explaining reasons. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Recent cases show that people don't like relying on AI and prefer to trust human experts, even if these experts are wrong.
If we want AI to really benefit people, we need to find a way to get people to trust it.
To do that, we need to understand why people are so reluctant to trust AI in the first place.
Take the case of Watson for Oncology, one of technology giant IBM's supercomputer programs.
Their attempt to promote this program to cancer doctors was a PR disaster.
items.explain: Q28: The passage describes how IBM's Watson program was a *'PR disaster'* when promoted to doctors — **'PR disaster'** means a public failure. This matches heading **vi** — *'Widespread distrust of an AI innovation'* — where **'distrust'** means lack of trust. So the answer is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: The AI promised to deliver top-quality recommendations on the treatment of 12 cancers that accounted for 80% of the world's cases.
But when doctors first interacted with Watson, they found themselves in a rather difficult situation.
On the one hand, if Watson provided guidance about a treatment that coincided with their own opinions, physicians did not see much point in Watson's recommendations.
The supercomputer was simply telling them what they already knew, and these recommendations did not change the actual treatment.
On the other hand, if Watson generated a recommendation that contradicted the experts' opinion, doctors would typically conclude that Watson wasn't competent.
And the machine wouldn't be able to explain why its treatment was plausible because its machine-learning algorithms were simply too complex to be fully understood by humans.
Consequently, this has caused even more suspicion and disbelief, leading many doctors to ignore the seemingly outlandish AI recommendations and stick to their own expertise.
This is just one example of people's lack of confidence in AI and their reluctance to accept what AI has to offer.
Trust in other people is often based on our understanding of how others think and having experience of their reliability.
items.explain: Q29: The passage explains that we trust people because we understand *'how others think'* and have *'experience of their reliability'*, but AI's process is *'too difficult for most people to comprehend'*. This matches heading **ii** — *'Reasons why we have more faith in human judgement than in AI'* — where **'faith'** means trust. So the answer is **ii**.

items.sentence_raw: This helps create a psychological feeling of safety.
AI, on the other hand, is still fairly new and unfamiliar to most people.
Even if it can be technically explained (and that's not always the case), AI's decision-making process is usually too difficult for most people to comprehend.
items.explain: Q29: The passage explains that we trust people because we understand *'how others think'* and have *'experience of their reliability'*, but AI's process is *'too difficult for most people to comprehend'*. This matches heading **ii** — *'Reasons why we have more faith in human judgement than in AI'* — where **'faith'** means trust. So the answer is **ii**.

items.sentence_raw: And interacting with something we don't understand can cause anxiety and give us a sense that we're losing control.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says interacting with AI we don't understand *'can cause anxiety and give us a sense that we're losing control'* — **'losing control'** means feeling at a disadvantage. This matches option **B** — *'Its complexity makes them feel that they are at a disadvantage'* — where **'complexity'** means difficulty to understand. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Many people are also simply not familiar with many instances of AI actually working, because it often happens in the background.
Instead, they are acutely aware of instances where AI goes wrong.
Embarrassing AI failures receive a disproportionate amount of media attention, emphasising the message that we cannot rely on technology.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says *'Embarrassing AI failures receive a disproportionate amount of media attention, emphasising the message that we cannot rely on technology'* — **'cannot rely on'** means to be mistrustful. This matches option **A** — *'It leads the public to be mistrustful of AI'* — where **'mistrustful'** means not trusting. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Machine learning is not foolproof, in part because the humans who design it aren't.
Feelings about AI run deep.
In a recent experiment, people from a range of backgrounds were given various sci-fi films about AI to watch and then asked questions about automation in everyday life.

It was found that, regardless of whether the film they watched depicted AI in a positive or negative light, simply watching a cinematic vision of our technological future polarised the participants' attitudes.
items.explain:
Q30: The passage says watching sci-fi films *'polarised the participants' attitudes'* — **'polarised'** means split into opposite groups. This matches heading **i** — *'An increasing divergence of attitudes towards AI'* — where **'divergence'** means growing apart. So the answer is **i**.

Q36: The passage says watching sci-fi films *'polarised the participants' attitudes'* — **'polarised'** means made existing opinions stronger, not changed them. The question says films *'make people change their opinions'* — ***'polarised' does NOT mean 'changed'***. These are different, so the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Optimists became more extreme in their enthusiasm for AI and sceptics became even more guarded.
This suggests people use relevant evidence about AI in a biased manner to support their existing attitudes, a deep-rooted human tendency known as "confirmation bias".
As AI is represented more and more in media and entertainment, it could lead to a society split between those who benefit from AI and those who reject it.
More pertinently, refusing to accept the advantages offered by AI could place a large group of people at a serious disadvantage.
items.explain: Q38: The passage says *'refusing to accept the advantages offered by AI could place a large group of people at a serious disadvantage'* — **'serious disadvantage'** means a negative effect on their lives. This directly matches the question statement that rejection *'may have a negative effect on many people's lives'*. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Fortunately, we already have some ideas about how to improve trust in AI.
Simply having previous experience with AI can significantly improve people's opinions about the technology, as was found in the study mentioned above.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says *'Simply having previous experience with AI can significantly improve people's opinions'* — **'significantly improve'** means a big impact, not very little. The question says familiarity has *'very little impact'* — ***'significantly improve' is the opposite of 'very little impact'***. These contradict, so the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Evidence also suggests the more you use other technologies such as the internet, the more you trust them.
Another solution may be to reveal more about the algorithms which AI uses and the purposes they serve.
items.explain: Q31: The passage suggests we should *'reveal more about the algorithms which AI uses'* — **'reveal'** means to show openly. This matches heading **vii** — *'Encouraging openness about how AI functions'* — where **'openness'** means being transparent. So the answer is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: Several high-profile social media companies and online marketplaces already release transparency reports about government requests and surveillance disclosures.
A similar practice for AI could help people have a better understanding of the way algorithmic decisions are made.
Research suggests that allowing people some control over AI decision-making could also improve trust and enable AI to learn from human experience.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says *'allowing people some control over AI decision-making could also improve trust'* — **'allowing people some control'** means involving users. This matches heading **v** — *'The advantages of involving users in AI processes'* — where **'involving users'** means giving them a role. So the answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: For example, one study showed that when people were allowed the freedom to slightly modify an algorithm, they felt more satisfied with its decisions, more likely to believe it was superior and more likely to use it in the future.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says when people could *'slightly modify an algorithm'*, they felt *'more satisfied'* and *'more likely to use it in the future'* — **'more satisfied'** means they approved more. This matches the question that modifiable applications *'are more likely to gain consumer approval'* — where **'approval'** means satisfaction. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: We don't need to understand the intricate inner workings of AI systems, but if people are given a degree of responsibility for how they are implemented, they will be more willing to accept AI into their lives.

orphan_explain_map.37: Q37: The passage discusses how media currently shows AI failures, but it never says whether future portrayals will become more positive or negative. ***The passage gives no information about future media trends*** — it only talks about the present. Since the passage neither confirms nor denies the statement, the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
